:question/math-academy-id "e-3240" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078537 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eaac3fe1-285b-57ba-956b-66eaf51ded7e" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Trigonometric Ratios Given a Triangle with Integer Side Lengths"}] :question/problem "Find $\sin{\theta}$, $\cos{\theta}$, and $\tan{\theta}$ for the triangle below.

![](images/ed/ed11931671711d754241c84981e7cebf12f04bdae56a1c8b26a194a6bf44b7ca.png)" :question/worked-solution "Remember the acronym "SOH-CAH-TOA."

- The sine of an angle is equal to the opposite divided by the hypotenuse (S-O-H). Relative to the angle $\theta$, the opposite side is $\overline{AC}$, and the hypotenuse is $\overline{BC}$. Therefore,
$\sin{\theta} = \dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.
- The cosine of an angle is equal to the adjacent divided by the hypotenuse (C-A-H). Relative to the angle $\theta$, the adjacent side is $\overline{AB}$, and the hypotenuse is $\overline{BC}$. Therefore,
$\cos{\theta} = \dfrac{AB}{BC} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.
- The tangent of an angle is equal to the opposite divided by the adjacent (T-O-A). Relative to the angle $\theta$, the opposite side is $\overline{AC}$, and the adjacent side is $\overline{AB}$. Therefore,
$\tan{\theta} = \dfrac{AC}{AB} = \dfrac{3}{4}$."} {:db/id 17592186050876} {:db/id 17592186078724 :question/id #uuid "918aabe8-38b2-5fea-9ef1-3f6952bdadaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-121617"} {:db/id 17592186078838 :question/id #uuid "366c2e37-c69f-54a4-a46f-285ff36fdcca" :question/math-academy-id "q-263317"} {:db/id 17592186079106 :question/id #uuid "bb07278b-3c66-5c55-a1eb-081fe90710b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-54055"} {:db/id 17592186078538 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078253 :question/id #uuid "c9ac49b1-04df-5cf0-bd38-3bc5b044b612" :question/math-academy-id "e-3245"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "50c8132c-18c7-5250-a68e-68500bdb926e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048702}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078813 :question/id #uuid "95f1251e-15f5-54b6-8b77-ad83cc5d0afd" :question/math-academy-id "q-241911"} {:db/id 17592186078814 :question/id #uuid "cffc5266-e6df-552f-b984-f315cd270ba8" :question/math-academy-id "q-241912"} {:db/id 17592186079109 :question/id #uuid "17b3409e-c61c-5642-bdba-0650252b6236" :question/math-academy-id "q-54108"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio Given a Triangle with Non-Integer Side Lengths"} {:db/id 17592186078253 :question/id #uuid "c9ac49b1-04df-5cf0-bd38-3bc5b044b612" :question/math-academy-id "e-3245" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078538 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "50c8132c-18c7-5250-a68e-68500bdb926e" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio Given a Triangle with Non-Integer Side Lengths"}] :question/problem "In the right triangle $\triangle ABC$, the angle $\angle A$ is a right angle, and the side lengths are $AB=2$, $AC=\sqrt{5}$, and $BC=3$. Find $\tan B$." :question/worked-solution "Let's illustrate the given triangle.

![](images/4e/4e4e2005e31716a09953aed9054cc5796ee915d41d5a9020042984b348e3b743.png)

The tangent of an angle is equal to the opposite divided by the adjacent (T-O-A). Relative to $\angle B$, the opposite side is $\overline{AC}$, and the adjacent side is $\overline{AB}$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned} \tan{B} &= \dfrac{AC}{AB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}. \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048702} {:db/id 17592186078813 :question/id #uuid "95f1251e-15f5-54b6-8b77-ad83cc5d0afd" :question/math-academy-id "q-241911"} {:db/id 17592186078814 :question/id #uuid "cffc5266-e6df-552f-b984-f315cd270ba8" :question/math-academy-id "q-241912"} {:db/id 17592186079109 :question/id #uuid "17b3409e-c61c-5642-bdba-0650252b6236" :question/math-academy-id "q-54108"} {:db/id 17592186078539 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078251 :question/id #uuid "e012dbd0-341b-5f01-a670-539c472471bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-3243"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b6359c90-3e3e-54f3-a66b-c8f69058a3a3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048144}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078839 :question/id #uuid "d560e0be-34af-5aa8-aafd-31445ea84967" :question/math-academy-id "q-264136"} {:db/id 17592186078844 :question/id #uuid "75295c98-9514-533e-816c-54d052780916" :question/math-academy-id "q-28037"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving for a Variable Given a Trigonometric Ratio"} {:db/id 17592186078251 :question/id #uuid "e012dbd0-341b-5f01-a670-539c472471bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-3243" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078539 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b6359c90-3e3e-54f3-a66b-c8f69058a3a3" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for a Variable Given a Trigonometric Ratio"}] :question/problem "Given that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}$, find the value of $x$.

![](images/f8/f8affbac78c75000d7bbbc8c15508252f7bea0270fdf6cc9c5e5244eb89b505d.png)" :question/worked-solution "The tangent of an angle is equal to the opposite divided by the adjacent (T-O-A).

Relative to the angle $\theta$, the length of the opposite side is $x-1$, and the length of the adjacent side is $2x$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan θ &= \frac{opposite}{adjacent} \\
\frac{1}{4} &= \frac{x - 1}{2x} \\
2x &= 4(x - 1) \\
2x &= 4x - 4 \\
2x &= 4 \\
x &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048144} {:db/id 17592186078839 :question/id #uuid "d560e0be-34af-5aa8-aafd-31445ea84967" :question/math-academy-id "q-264136"} {:db/id 17592186078844 :question/id #uuid "75295c98-9514-533e-816c-54d052780916" :question/math-academy-id "q-28037"} {:db/id 17592186078540 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078255 :question/id #uuid "81f7e0c1-99bf-5feb-9db2-745595a8b613" :question/math-academy-id "e-3247"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bcbd6c22-13de-5a61-90b0-38bd478b4f2f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048438}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078815 :question/id #uuid "038037ad-fb97-59e8-bf2f-0b6bd95242af" :question/math-academy-id "q-241915"} {:db/id 17592186079107 :question/id #uuid "92589d7c-66d5-5d06-8ff8-401006025c34" :question/math-academy-id "q-54066"} {:db/id 17592186079108 :question/id #uuid "70ac9718-4946-550a-9d69-2d46bc10669e" :question/math-academy-id "q-54103"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Function Using a Calculator"} {:db/id 17592186078255 :question/id #uuid "81f7e0c1-99bf-5feb-9db2-745595a8b613" :question/math-academy-id "e-3247" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078540 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bcbd6c22-13de-5a61-90b0-38bd478b4f2f" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Function Using a Calculator"}] :question/problem "Evaluate $\cos\left(50^\circ\right)$. ![](images/4c/4cbe48f70bc4bf67600269883c1260cec2181cf01b50a9675c3177b72d7f954b.png)

The three fundamental trigonometric ratios, **sine**, **cosine**, and **tangent**, represent the ratios of the sides of a right triangle. The ratios are often shortened to $\sin$, $\cos$, and $\tan$, and they are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned} \sin(\theta) &= \dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}, \\[5pt] \cos(\theta) &= \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}, \\[5pt] \tan(\theta) &= \dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{adjacent}}. \end{aligned}
$$

For a given angle $\theta$, these ratios remain the same no matter what the size of the triangle is. For example, if we were to double the length of each side of a given triangle, the values of these ratios would remain unchanged.

An easy way of remembering how to compute the different trigonometric ratios is by using the three-syllable acronym **SOH-CAH-TOA**. It stands for:

- SOH $\rightarrow$ **S**ine = **O**pposite / **H**ypotenuse,
- CAH $\rightarrow$ **C**osine = **A**djacent / **H**ypotenuse,
- TOA $\rightarrow$ **T**angent = **O**pposite / **A**djacent." :tutorial/id #uuid "7210f33b-b202-57e9-a4c7-8eb1859c0b97" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2445 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid For example, using a calculator, we can compute the trigonometric ratios for

$$
\theta = 30^\circ
$$

and get the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin (30^{∘}) &= 0.5 \\
\cos (30^{∘}) &= 0.866... \\
\tan (30^{∘}) &= 0.577..
\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/4c/4cbe48f70bc4bf67600269883c1260cec2181cf01b50a9675c3177b72d7f954b.png)

The three fundamental trigonometric ratios, **sine**, **cosine**, and **tangent**, represent the ratios of the sides of a right triangle. The ratios are often shortened to $\sin$, $\cos$, and $\tan$, and they are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned} \sin(\theta) &= \dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}, \\[5pt] \cos(\theta) &= \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}, \\[5pt] \tan(\theta) &= \dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{adjacent}}. \end{aligned}
$$

For a given angle $\theta$, these ratios remain the same no matter what the size of the triangle is. For example, if we were to double the length of each side of a given triangle, the values of these ratios would remain unchanged.

An easy way of remembering how to compute the different trigonometric ratios is by using the three-syllable acronym **SOH-CAH-TOA**. It stands for:

- SOH $\rightarrow$ **S**ine = **O**pposite / **H**ypotenuse,
- CAH $\rightarrow$ **C**osine = **A**djacent / **H**ypotenuse,
- TOA $\rightarrow$ **T**angent = **O**pposite / **A**djacent." :tutorial/id #uuid "7210f33b-b202-57e9-a4c7-8eb1859c0b97" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2445 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e8abd38-6d6c-5110-8d68-959bdff3fee0" :step/math-academy-id 454273 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079472}} {:db/id 17592186079636 :tutorial/content "Let's remind ourselves of the names of the sides of a right triangle relative to an angle $\theta$.

:question/problem "Given that $\,A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-4A+I) & =O \\ A-4I+{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =4I-A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4,$ $q=-1$ and

$$
p+q=4+(-1)=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186323945 :question/id #uuid "5734eef3-bee7-5a34-ab88-0e69bc193d36" :question/math-academy-id "q-37831"} {:db/id 17592186326708 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{3}+(-\frac{1}{6})=\frac{7}{6}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186326811 :question/id #uuid "0d383f46-698f-5924-8d8d-4466dfa087b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-40168" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17bf09fd-3fd5-5fa9-bd7c-9bb8300133ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{3}{2}{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186324178} {:answer/id #uuid "2196ad3b-dc18-575d-9ac5-f3e82f2cf1f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186324248} {:answer/id #uuid "ae47339b-004d-5c20-8d9d-8aab1f4f98f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2I-A-2{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186325449} {:answer/id #uuid "bc9f773a-008b-571e-8538-a3402ba6e607" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}I-\frac{7}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186325590} {:answer/id #uuid "d899671a-8147-5a25-9c47-966430b53806" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9I-A-{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186325855}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324248} :answer-field/id #uuid "f00c9e90-925d-5d82-b4f9-f2d77c2b5637" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326651}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix},$ then ${A}^{-1}=$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$

$$

:question/problem "Given that $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 7\end{bmatrix},$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$" :question/worked-solution "The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2} &=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} &=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot 7-(-4)\cdot 3 \\  & =35+12 \\  & =47.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549986 :question/id #uuid "a0915342-2d27-50ea-9893-ae57d8dcc177" :question/math-academy-id "q-83392"} {:db/id 17592186050054} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1972} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125429 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125794 :tutorial/content "The characteristic equation of a square matrix $A$ is given by 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

On the left-hand side of this equation, we have the expression 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I),
$$

 which we call the **characteristic polynomial** of the matrix $A.$

For instance, let's find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix ![](images/1d/1d6d0bdedbb25bbc41759e443cdc0f6a207ef5cbfa4761b05e1a1a2eda24cbec.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(C-\lambda I) \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| \\  & =(-8-\lambda )\cdot (7-\lambda )-(-9)\cdot 6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25396b96-19ec-592d-b1c4-3c6fa172ef08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3580 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9083e01a-4e57-589b-9b08-48ecc4af0075" :step/math-academy-id 20133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125433}} {:db/id 17592186125430 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following: 

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.
$$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](images/d2/d24f480293267a9ddc28b03626e7bde6f01bd62a136fed17f8580bf1ea34d776.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is

![](images/8e/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "f3faf291-dd20-56c9-bc3d-8482113b6764" :step/math-academy-id 21546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125430}} {:db/id 17592186125502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this." :tutorial/id #uuid "769ceb10-1667-52b6-8a89-b4c7ca835276" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4448 :tutorial/title "Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "3167e19f-42e7-5fc7-8ee9-fb73a5fa3da3" :step/math-academy-id 27370 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125434}}] :activity/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124757} {:db/id 17592186125429 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125794 :tutorial/content "The characteristic equation of a square matrix $A$ is given by

Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "0fed3d43-139d-505f-8482-70f3be0516d6" :step/math-academy-id 20138} {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this." :tutorial/id #uuid "769ceb10-1667-52b6-8a89-b4c7ca835276" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4448 :tutorial/title "Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186440844} :activity/id #uuid "08986419-9a71-537f-9305-f8e778b26413" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048726 :topic/id #uuid "b8f25367-71a5-50d2-9e6e-d239937a1fac" :topic/math-academy-id 1972} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186440842 :step/content {:db/id 17592186354446 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b7c0e75-3d49-5406-9041-ede1d5bfdf47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186351962} {:answer/id #uuid "33bb1eb5-07b0-5c72-9e4a-a39b341c088c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{4}" :db/id 17592186352048} {:answer/id #uuid "6b960fbb-7fd4-564b-88d9-596a86197fe5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{8}" :db/id 17592186352519} {:answer/id #uuid "a471234f-1f9f-56ed-9886-d314b4205faa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{8}" :db/id 17592186352971} {:answer/id #uuid "e3378a1b-e1c9-5e1d-b90b-a6157d273dbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186353544}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186351962} :answer-field/id #uuid "ba728d29-f974-5f4e-bf33-9c1c26f466d1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186354136}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "83ac805a-2248-5c38-94ec-8370eb490b39" :question/math-academy-id "q-85928" :question/problem "Given that $\,A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{8},$ $q=-\frac{1}{8}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{8}+(-\frac{1}{8})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "37974a8d-1c28-54c7-b296-b5b3c2e14d09" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440845}} {:db/id 17592186440843 :step/content {:db/id 17592186354443 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23996cc9-567a-51b9-98b0-2f94757720ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{A}^{2}-3A+16I" :db/id 17592186351889} {:answer/id #uuid "3b9440a6-7475-5119-a281-5c4281a46f22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{A}^{2}-3A+6I" :db/id 17592186352117} {:answer/id #uuid "a1e14de5-77a9-57b7-8420-3ce37cbf93ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3A-16I" :db/id 17592186352952} {:answer/id #uuid "b5a9477d-b279-5e07-bb55-bcddccdb5c4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{A}^{2}+3A-16I" :db/id 17592186353124} {:answer/id #uuid "dedacf6f-daed-557d-84e3-a6bbb9be9999" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3A+16I" :db/id 17592186353503}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186351889} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb1e7ca4-8013-510f-a476-bdfe0c462d57" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186354164}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "03d6fc6a-0f72-5d35-ba67-c4e4d25be4dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-85924" :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix with the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{3}-{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -16.$ Then, ${A}^{3}=$" :question/worked-solution "Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{3}-{A}^{2}+3A-16I & =O \\ {A}^{3} & ={A}^{2}-3A+16I.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "864708dc-01cf-5025-81a5-3d649155dedc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440842}} {:db/id 17592186440844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326708 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28cc5ee2-6da9-52c1-a92b-8edb26634139" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{6}" :db/id 17592186324300} {:answer/id #uuid "47e93b3f-33d7-5090-b1fc-02844e927bff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{6}" :db/id 17592186324553} {:answer/id #uuid "a44579f4-a9e4-53da-a506-9eefbb4bf2e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186325367} {:answer/id #uuid "bd8f6f17-d42e-553d-a74b-0e76268b5611" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186325601} {:answer/id #uuid "d1b95922-aad1-5b77-a0d0-e6a698ab713b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186325792}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324300} :answer-field/id #uuid "36035083-9336-58a8-9968-10256743cb12" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326311}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "688a2834-9fcd-5275-97a0-97e7aaa1b79c" :question/math-academy-id "q-38704" :question/problem "Given that $\,A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{3}+(-\frac{1}{6})=\frac{7}{6}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8b979659-38ec-5258-8754-0f5aa34455d5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440843}} {:db/id 17592186440845 :step/content {:db/id 17592186354451 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1c632238-e62f-5f74-b0da-ba8a2b7c7882" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}21 & 0 \\ 72 & -27\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186351821} {:answer/id #uuid "470c7209-55c8-5c45-abce-7fe3f84f4c6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}21 & 27 \\ 0 & -72\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186352224} {:answer/id #uuid "5e13d16b-8e89-589c-b83e-8c447ea31fb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}27 & 72 \\ 0 & -21\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186352401} {:answer/id #uuid "ad3d6b3f-3399-57a6-94b9-b1ab92b58f8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}21 & 72 \\ 0 & -27\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186353035} {:answer/id #uuid "dd1b1292-04d5-5403-8881-a67fccaa7676" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}12 & 72 \\ 0 & -12\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186353490}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186353035} :answer-field/id #uuid "af398d18-f5a4-5a12-bc2f-96080c170593" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186354125}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e1de5236-83e9-5753-abb0-71abaf264e50" :question/math-academy-id "q-85993" :question/problem "Given the matrix
$\,A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 12 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}$
and $f(x)={x}^{21}-16{x}^{19}+6x-3$, find $f(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 12 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda ) \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">${x}^{21}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$16{x}^{19}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
</tr>
<tr>

<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$6x$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$3$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(6x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{19}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(6A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(6A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(6A-3I) \\  & =6A-3I \\  & =6\begin{bmatrix}4 & 12 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}24 & 72 \\ 0 & -24\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}21 & 72 \\ 0 & -27\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9ee92d90-8ec9-5c83-abd0-9bf2b158360d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440846}} {:db/id 17592186440846 :step/content {:db/id 17592186272142 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "025a5c1a-4f6e-5e42-8dce-96a2fd08178a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}25 & -42 \\ 14 & -31\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186269289} {:answer/id #uuid "23310913-8cd2-557c-be76-7e2691fe0ee4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}31 & 14 \\ 42 & -25\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186269575} {:answer/id #uuid "9142a6e7-f5cb-5d0d-bcaf-2c7c6f384044" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}15 & 14 \\ -42 & 30\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186270533} {:answer/id #uuid "efb97e7a-5224-5bc1-9035-2d0d54445cd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}25 & 12 \\ -24 & -31\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186271376} {:answer/id #uuid "f7416ab1-633c-5a86-bade-cffdf59d2d02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186271438}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186271438} :answer-field/id #uuid "8d72f403-dcf6-5b06-9505-8ae246f18a3e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186271759}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "af2db92b-ede0-52d7-a7d4-1043a63d9db0" :question/math-academy-id "q-140602" :question/problem "Given the matrix

and $\,f(x)={x}^{16}-4{x}^{14}+7x-3\,$, find $f(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

<td align="left" colspan="7" height="20" width="20">$\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$</td>
</tr>
<tr>

<td align="center" height="20" width="20">${x}^{16}$</td>

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-4A+I) & =O \\ A-4I+{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =4I-A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4,$ $q=-1$ and

$$
p+q=4+(-1)=3.

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\  & =-2A+6I \\  & =-2\begin{bmatrix}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{bmatrix}+6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2} &=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} &=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot 7-(-4)\cdot 3 \\  & =35+12 \\  & =47.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f73f0739-b0b6-5a0b-9fac-ab5fdff3e3e1"}] :activity/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186485755} {:db/id 17592186486487 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323940 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d94a386-0e3f-5fd6-82d2-7e3b9d7cbeec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186321252} {:answer/id #uuid "2cbc3e40-f109-58b8-872a-95626283c9f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186321493} {:answer/id #uuid "389d0b0e-b88a-5ab8-9fa3-85ae37139eee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186321578} {:answer/id #uuid "73fc0bbe-4d33-5b94-bad1-7a748598633e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186322053} {:answer/id #uuid "f9936d7e-e12d-5d02-a132-90f3f19d81e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186323111}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321252} :answer-field/id #uuid "399304a9-7f1c-5273-8e27-ae2b68d805f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323284}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a72555f5-f964-563d-a2c6-2e5bad5e5508" :question/math-academy-id "q-37778" :question/problem "Given that $\,A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

:question/math-academy-id "q-140520" :question/problem "Given that $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 7\end{bmatrix},$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$" :question/worked-solution "The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2} &=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} &=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot 7-(-4)\cdot 3 \\  & =35+12 \\  & =47.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f73f0739-b0b6-5a0b-9fac-ab5fdff3e3e1"} {:db/id 17592186486479 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125140 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "486030d8-debf-5bf3-8646-937755b93331" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2A+{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186324558} {:answer/id #uuid "7cb39a68-d9fa-5afc-a46e-1646bc050802" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{A}^{2}-A" :db/id 17592186325023} {:answer/id #uuid "8f700b32-f8f5-50c2-8448-a2e3950f6cf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{A}^{2}-I" :db/id 17592186325188} {:answer/id #uuid "d2abfec0-1ad1-5263-bbad-6dc6f697cbf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2A-I" :db/id 17592186325799} {:answer/id #uuid "ec99ac0a-a7c2-59e7-88f3-37b0874d74a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2A-I" :db/id 17592186326052}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326052} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ae27e9b-e1c9-591e-ae97-64fbf12bf64f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326497}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "241347e1-d70b-502b-97bb-5ffa2634f0a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-38723" :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix with the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=-{\lambda }^{3}-2\lambda -1.$ Then, ${A}^{3}=$" :question/worked-solution "Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

:topic/math-academy-id 1045} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097454 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097919 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with fractional coefficients, such as the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 \\ 7x-5y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can turn the system into an equivalent system involving only integer coefficients. This will make it easier to solve.

In general, we multiply each equation by its lowest common denominator. In this instance, multiplying the first equation by the lowest common denominator of the fractions $(4)$ will do the job:

![](images/7f/7ff92bdf3b9c8bf5ffb571d598788f37bcd698f7b3971c337531bf9fe7f55e4e.svg)

Now, we can solve the system using, for example, the elimination method. Notice that the $5y$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-5y$ term in the second equation.

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable, and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\cancel{5y} & =-16 \\ 7x-\cancel{5y} & =-2 \\ 9x & =-18 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=-2$ into the equation $7x - 5y= -2$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-5y & =-2 \\ 7(-2)-5y & =-2 \\ -14-5y & =-2 \\ -5y & =12 \\ y & =-\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2, \,y=-\dfrac{12}{5}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68821d79-90e2-580a-95fd-a5268f848ff4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8706 :tutorial/title :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=4x(1-0.25x)-2xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-6y+3xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. The equilibria of the model are the following:

$(0,0),\,(${{field-1}}$,0),\,(${{field-2}}$,${{field-3}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2xy &=0 \\ -6y+3xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2x(0) & =0 \\ 4x(0.25x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(4,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2)(1-0.25(2))-2(2)y & =0 \\ 4-4y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2,1).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(4,0),\,(2,1).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186480667 :question/id #uuid "6f820e7d-e65e-5149-80bc-fca1cd9160a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-335587"} {:db/id 17592186480707 :question/id #uuid "f57e9bc6-8d1b-532c-906d-19c1ec051963" :question/math-academy-id "q-335608"} {:db/id 17592186497359 :question/id #uuid "54e98471-5688-5240-867b-3e9eae0b3046" :question/math-academy-id "q-335588" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ac7f7168-2238-5278-920a-322ccf51d756" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186497010}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186497010} :answer-field/id #uuid "2827ddbf-479b-5003-a2de-01715d6851fe" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186497233} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7038e05b-62e6-5b9d-89f6-5884cc66e3ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186496900}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496900} :answer-field/id #uuid "866fb4cc-629f-52ec-a9a5-882783d95536" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186497280} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "56c313eb-74f2-5951-b106-ca3f0b7a9669" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186496841}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496841} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9119afb-d7f2-5573-9b5d-ea702cbc65cd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186497295}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=4x(1-0.25x)-3xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-y+xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. The equilibria of the model are the following:

$(0,0),\,(${{field-1}}$,0),\,(${{field-2}}$,${{field-3}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-3xy &=0 \\ -y+xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-y+xy & =0 \\ y(-1+x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=1.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-3x(0) & =0 \\ 4x(0.25x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(4,0).$

- If $x=1,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4(1)(1-0.25(1))-3(1)y & =0 \\ 3-3y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(1,1).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)(1-0.5(1))-2(1)y & =0 \\ 1.5-2y & =0 \\ y & =0.75.\end{aligned}

Thus, another equilibrium is $(1,0.75).$

(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(1,0.75).

$$

$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=2-4x-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}2-4x-2y & -2x \\ 3y & -2+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4(0)-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 3(0) & -2+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ :topic/math-academy-id 3231} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167876 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168015 :tutorial/content "The Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with **carrying capacity** is given by 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, 

- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and

- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.

The only difference from the Lotka–Volterra model is the factor $(1-hx)$ in the prey equation. Notice that if $h=0,$ we get the standard model:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In our modified version of the model, the *intrinsic growth* of prey is given by the $ax(1-hx)$ term. Now, if there are no predators ($y=0$), then 

$$
x' = ax(1-hx).
$$

Recall that general solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,\frac{1}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{h}.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the *carrying capacity* (the limit the number of prey is approaching as $t$ goes to infinity).

:step/math-academy-id 590164 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167884}} {:db/id 17592186167879 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168016 :tutorial/content "Recall that the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

Notice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when 

$$
h < \dfrac{d}{c},
$$

which guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.

We now evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](images/89/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/f2/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get

![](images/b2/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)

Because we are considering the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that

$$
\dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Analyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/a7/a7673170825344e1831f2ba01ce4c20f10091380ff4e116f3b6bd9e7666e51aa.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ce000cd-7913-5e8e-90d2-3a5a820db4f4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14543 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Nonzero Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b61ca7e0-a217-5555-8d14-3f0d56453cb5" :step/math-academy-id 590167 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167885}} {:db/id 17592186167880 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166928 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166559 :question/id #uuid "3e280ec5-c95a-5ca6-ba2e-edc4cf653ea3" :question/math-academy-id "e-21736"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4936474f-5e5f-5da2-8242-1b48336a836c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048881}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167252} {:db/id 17592186167261} {:db/id 17592186370423} {:db/id 17592186370540} {:db/id 17592186480691} {:db/id 17592186497388}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case"} :step/id #uuid "33bb23bb-bd23-5d38-9487-0ff5ffdddc57" :step/math-academy-id 590168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167881}} {:db/id 17592186167881 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168017 :tutorial/content "Again, recall that the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

We have already considered the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ which guarantees that the third equilibrium will lie in the first quadrant. Let's now consider the remaining cases.

- When $h = \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium coincides with the second one. So, we have only two equilibria:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right) = \left(\dfrac{c}{d}, 0\right)
$$

- When $h > \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium is in the fourth quadrant (its $y$-coordinate is negative). So, we have only two equilibria that make sense in the context of the model:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

Hence, we get only two equilibria. 

The trajectories near the origin remain similar. However, the equilibrium at

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

will be an *asymptotically stable sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h \geq \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/b9/b94beebb63bc1312d56f655e48b3bc7cdb1b9badc5cdacd6b88b073c5055adc9.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/cd/cd60f32a5daff3c805b097d121814d19e04781ed1bcfead989cde82db674e5d9.png)

Eventually, the *predators go extinct* while the prey approaches the carrying capacity of the system.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy &=0 \\ -cy+dxy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79e78f76-a29e-544f-a86b-9f714e69cf63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14597 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} :step/id #uuid "f7c2a3b7-bd87-5cba-ba5e-ea5beeed7071" :step/math-academy-id 590177 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167878}} {:db/id 17592186167884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168029 :tutorial/content "Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :tutorial/id #uuid "feef6e7a-79a2-5b71-8cec-dc45e305ec52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14598 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "8118c930-2041-5a97-bb4f-5812d27ead9b" :step/math-academy-id 590178 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167879}} {:db/id 17592186167885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168030 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=4x(1-0.25x)-xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-2y+3xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We'll evaluate its Jacobian at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[4, \, 0]^T$ that lies on the $x$-axis.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-0.25x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=4-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/0b/0bd1edc4527b82bebf84d38f8d4a79b65062d6b38c5fa4c84b7509acaa547f42.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/30/30463f939876ccbee7cf77f8fdc80fb4e8a27fe0ad5af22cd51e1be3433a3af5.svg) to get

![](images/fc/fc40e7e568705e08b70e0dedae710b2e8514837491730ae12a90bed764261f97.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = 10$ and $\lambda_2=-4$. Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, 

- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and

- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.

The only difference from the Lotka–Volterra model is the factor $(1-hx)$ in the prey equation. Notice that if $h=0,$ we get the standard model:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In our modified version of the model, the *intrinsic growth* of prey is given by the $ax(1-hx)$ term. Now, if there are no predators ($y=0$), then 

$$
x' = ax(1-hx).
$$

Recall that general solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,\frac{1}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{h}.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the *carrying capacity* (the limit the number of prey is approaching as $t$ goes to infinity).

$$

\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

Notice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when 

$$
h < \dfrac{d}{c},
$$

which guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.

We now evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](images/89/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/f2/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get

![](images/b2/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)

Because we are considering the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that

$$
\dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Analyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

We have already considered the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ which guarantees that the third equilibrium will lie in the first quadrant. Let's now consider the remaining cases.

- When $h = \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium coincides with the second one. So, we have only two equilibria:

$$

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

Hence, we get only two equilibria. 

The trajectories near the origin remain similar. However, the equilibrium at

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

will be an *asymptotically stable sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h \geq \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/b9/b94beebb63bc1312d56f655e48b3bc7cdb1b9badc5cdacd6b88b073c5055adc9.png)

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/cd/cd60f32a5daff3c805b097d121814d19e04781ed1bcfead989cde82db674e5d9.png)

Eventually, the *predators go extinct* while the prey approaches the carrying capacity of the system.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy &=0 \\ -cy+dxy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79e78f76-a29e-544f-a86b-9f714e69cf63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14597 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} {:db/id 17592186168029 :tutorial/content "Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :tutorial/id #uuid "feef6e7a-79a2-5b71-8cec-dc45e305ec52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14598 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} {:db/id 17592186168030 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=2-4x-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}2-4x-2y & -2x \\ 3y & -2+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4(0)-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 3(0) & -2+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x(1-2x)-xy)=5-20x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}5-20x-y & -x \\ 3y & -2+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}5-20(0)-0 & -0 \\ 3(0) & -2+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6734dc20-5e4c-5ba3-a922-996f26cded96" :question/math-academy-id "q-335607" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=4x(1-0.25x)-2xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-6y+3xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. The equilibria of the model are the following:

$(0,0),\,(${{field-1}}$,0),\,(${{field-2}}$,${{field-3}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2xy &=0 \\ -6y+3xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2x(0) & =0 \\ 4x(0.25x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(4,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2)(1-0.25(2))-2(2)y & =0 \\ 4-4y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2,1).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(4,0),\,(2,1).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9c6eefcd-5b2a-58f2-8fa4-3bbf0349123c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497435}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b0cca672-22d2-56b4-8615-61d6e24b7f94" :answer/type {:db/id Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=3-1.8x-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=-4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+xy)=-1+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}3-1.8x-4y & -4x \\ y & -1+x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}3-1.8(0)-4(0) & -4(0) \\ 0 & -1+0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x(1-0.5x)-2xy &=0 \\ -4y+4xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4y+4xy & =0 \\ y(-4+4x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=1.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3x(1-0.5x)-2x(0) & =0 \\ 3x(0.5x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(2,0).$

- If $x=1,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)(1-0.5(1))-2(1)y & =0 \\ 1.5-2y & =0 \\ y & =0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(1,0.75).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(1,0.75).

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=3-1.8x-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=-4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+xy)=-1+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}3-1.8x-4y & -4x \\ y & -1+x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}3-1.8(0)-4(0) & -4(0) \\ 0 & -1+0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $csc⁡\theta .$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/44/44a555d222e3f6ff85208e8722a728ad240c558de7982d2a480bf9ddfb23ac6f.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{15}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{10}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.$

Knowing that $csc⁡\theta =\frac{1}{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}csc⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5})}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}csc⁡\theta  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{10}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{10}}{10} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186354407 :question/id #uuid "5348ffc1-6c19-57de-8e72-a13dbe8b5969" :question/math-academy-id "q-85234"} {:db/id 17592186541076 :question/id #uuid We can then draw a right triangle, where the hypotenuse is the line segment between the origin and the point. 

![](images/4b/4bae3a49b5557df9e5b50280d744aa72048b2d224df042e103a6b5d156467de7.png)

Since the hypotenuse is the radius of the unit circle, its length must be equal to $1.$ And, since the triangle is a right triangle, the $(x,y)$ coordinates of any point on the unit circle in the first quadrant must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
x^2+y^2=1.
$$

We can use this to find the $y$-coordinate of a point given the $x$-coordinate, and vice-versa.

For example, suppose that the $x$-coordinate of a point $P$ in the first quadrant on the unit circle is $\dfrac{3}{7}.$ To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=\dfrac{3}{7}$ into the above and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		x^2+y^2&=1\[5pt]
	          \left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2+y^2&=1\[5pt]
		\dfrac{9}{49}+y^2&=1\[5pt]
		y^2&= 1-\dfrac{9}{49}\[5pt]
		y^2&= \dfrac{40}{49}\[5pt]
		y&= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{40}{49}}\[5pt]
	        y &= \pm \dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}

}
$$

Since $P$ lies in the first quadrant, $y$ must be positive. So we select the positive answer. 

Therefore, our final answer is $y=\dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4029eb2-0222-5d8b-a285-7f0089655736" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2718 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "91d91920-7585-54d5-a3bb-aa4f02c97c17" :step/math-academy-id 87629 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111736}} {:db/id 17592186111736 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110754 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110456 :question/id #uuid "42313322-7535-5969-ad84-958449e48c1b" :question/math-academy-id "e-3480"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "87c18ea8-af12-52bd-8420-ec24ed63de65" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049224}] :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186510724} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110987} {:db/id 17592186111340} {:db/id 17592186259693} {:db/id 17592186259694} {:db/id 17592186259695} {:db/id 17592186290449} {:db/id 17592186335778}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle"} :step/id #uuid "51014196-5277-5ae7-8d38-8cacaa66b4eb" :step/math-academy-id 87630 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111737}} {:db/id 17592186111737 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111867 :tutorial/content "Recall that the coordinates of a point on the unit circle with a central angle $\theta$ have the property

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

If this point is in the first quadrant, we can substitute these values into the Pythagorean Identity from before to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The last expression is known as the **Pythagorean trigonometric identity,** and is arguably the most important equation in trigonometry.

The Pythagorean trigonometric identity holds for *every* angle $\theta,$ not just if $\theta$ is in the first quadrant. In this lesson, we're focusing on the first quadrant only. \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The last expression is known as the **Pythagorean trigonometric identity,** and is arguably the most important equation in trigonometry.

The Pythagorean trigonometric identity holds for *every* angle $\theta,$ not just if $\theta$ is in the first quadrant. In this lesson, we're focusing on the first quadrant only. :question/math-academy-id "e-4687" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186129113 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f5d1d859-0b86-5507-a7bf-3d805a85adf3" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Augmented Matrices in Row Echelon Form"}] :question/problem "Which of the following augmented matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right].
$$

" :question/worked-solution "Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The first matrix is not in row echelon form since $a_{32} \neq 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The second matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & -2 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 7\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The third matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & -1 & 4 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 0\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The fourth matrix is not in row echelon form since, for example, the leading entry $a_{22}$ lies to the left of the leading entry $a_{13}$ (condition II is violated).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 1 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}1}} & {\color{black}0} & 1 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}1}} & {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}1} & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & -4 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 7\end{array}\right]

$$

"2d390841-351e-54f5-ad19-90b6ebae5799" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form"}] :question/problem "Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B= \begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 7 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
C= \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

" :question/worked-solution "Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 1 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B= \begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 7 & 10 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C= \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 3 & 6 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{4} & 8\end{bmatrix}
$$
