:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186158091 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158432 :tutorial/content "We can extend a scalar function $f(x)$ to a square matrix argument $A.$ This function $f(A)$ is called a **matrix function**, and maps a square matrix to another square matrix of the same size.

Given a square matrix $A$ and a scalar function $f$ with Maclaurin series

$$
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k,
$$

we can define $f(A)$ by replacing $x$ with $A,$ with addition and multiplication performed in the matrix sense:

$$
f(A) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k A^k
$$

For example, recall that the Maclaurin series of $f(x) = e^x$ is

$$
e^x = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \dfrac{x^k}{k!}.
$$

Then, for a square matrix $A,$ we define the matrix exponential as

$$
e^A = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \dfrac{1}{k!}A^k.
$$

In the next slide, we'll see how to apply matrix functions to square matrices." :tutorial/id #uuid "c3451824-f52b-539c-b16f-3819d3ea37df" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10688 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "215d5365-8c77-5734-bfe7-0ac93d99aa62" :step/math-academy-id 231906 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158092}} {:db/id 17592186158092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158433 :tutorial/content "Suppose $D$ is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}\end{bmatrix}
$$

For a scalar function $f$ with a Maclaurin series expansion, $f(D)$ is the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $f(\lambda_1), \ldots, f(\lambda_n){:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}f({\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & f({\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{bmatrix}
$$

For example, given the matrix
$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
and the function $f(x) = e^x,$ we have

$$
\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & 0 \\ 0 & f(1)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This rule works because raising a diagonal matrix to a power is equivalent to raising each diagonal entry to the same power.

Indeed, if
$\displaystyle
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k$
is the Maclaurin series of $f,$ then, by the definition of $f(D),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(D) & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{D}^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}\end{bmatrix}}^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}^{k}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{n}^{k}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}f({\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & f({\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da162714-f641-5ded-aec8-6f24c0d5cbb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10689 :tutorial/title "Function of a Diagonal Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "c8b4e298-ed67-50ea-bb52-8968e4cd58bf" :step/math-academy-id 231907 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158093}} {:db/id 17592186158093 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157268 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157036 :question/id #uuid "5cba0e13-0b34-568b-8a69-eac3fced6338" :question/math-academy-id "e-16515"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "343f8efc-fdef-51dc-ad3f-fad1ab37bc88" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050446} {:db/id 17592186050812}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157695} {:db/id 17592186157699} {:db/id 17592186292544} {:db/id 17592186292545} {:db/id 17592186292546} {:db/id 17592186292552}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Function of a Diagonal Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "91d86e1a-5d29-5149-9978-86770afc6de0" :step/math-academy-id 231908 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158094}} {:db/id 17592186158094 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158434 :tutorial/content "Suppose $J_n(\lambda)$ is an $n\times n$ Jordan block where the main diagonal entries are all $\lambda{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda  & 1 & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda  & 1 & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & \lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

For a scalar function $f$ analytic at $\lambda$ (i.e., has a Taylor series expansion at $\lambda$), $f(J_n(\lambda))$ is the matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{''}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}
$$

To demonstrate, let's find $f(J_3(2))$ for $f(x) = \ln x.$

Since $J_3(2)$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, we will need the first $3-1=2$ derivatives of $f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}x \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{''}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

![](images/43/439d1a1c3c2c315510fd293e8bb8e1467e149222025359a0e0d899270eb07e12.svg)

Now that we can compute the value of a function of a Jordan block, we can also find the value of a function of a Jordan matrix.

The matrix [math]f(J_n(\lambda))[/math] for [math]n=2,3,[/math] and [math]4[/math] are as follows.

* For [math]2\times 2[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_2(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

* For [math]3\times 3[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_3(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

* For [math]4\times 4[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_4(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) & \dfrac16f'''(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & 0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]" :tutorial/id #uuid "7972371e-9205-5e74-b277-6dfcab332f9b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10691 :tutorial/title "Function of a Jordan Block"} :step/id #uuid "deee50a7-b19c-5fb9-80a5-a024ec3943c0" :step/math-academy-id 231911 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158424}} {:db/id 17592186158095 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157269 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157037 :question/id #uuid "f2d8972a-4337-5608-9c82-6fb5e74d22c7" :question/math-academy-id "e-16516"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8ce12d6f-8d1c-52f3-992f-534b9d91dda9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048640}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157696} {:db/id 17592186157700} {:db/id 17592186292547} {:db/id 17592186292553} {:db/id 17592186292554} {:db/id 17592186363586} {:db/id 17592186363595} {:db/id 17592186377004} {:db/id 17592186414003} {:db/id 17592186414006}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Block"} :step/id #uuid "c9bdde30-6bf2-5ffc-93a3-92c41bf6792d" :step/math-academy-id 231912 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158096}} {:db/id 17592186158096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157270 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157039 :question/id #uuid "2bd13883-8376-54f1-9985-83b95f1062a5" :question/math-academy-id "e-16522"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "87883002-67eb-5111-b15a-c5941bb33f9b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157697} {:db/id 17592186157698} {:db/id 17592186292562} {:db/id 17592186292563} {:db/id 17592186292564} {:db/id 17592186363654} {:db/id 17592186363665} {:db/id 17592186377013} {:db/id 17592186377024} {:db/id 17592186414005}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "f4444ff2-15d1-524f-952e-a3223b79ead3" :step/math-academy-id 231915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158097}} {:db/id 17592186158097 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158435 :tutorial/content "Suppose $A$ and $S$ are matrices, where $S$ is invertible.
For a scalar function $f$ with a Maclaurin series expansion, we have

$$
f(SAS^{-1}) = Sf(A)S^{-1}.
$$

Indeed, given the Maclaurin series $\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_kx^k,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(SA{S}^{-1}) & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}(SA{S}^{-1})^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}S{A}^{k}{S}^{-1} \\  & =S({\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{A}^{k}){S}^{-1} \\  & =Sf(A){S}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So far, we have seen how to evaluate functions for diagonal matrices and Jordan blocks. With the formula above, we will now be able to

- evaluate $f(B)$ for diagonalizable $B$ using a diagonalization $B=PDP^{-1},$ and

- evaluate $f(B)$ for non-diagonalizable $B$ using a Jordan decomposition $B=PJP^{-1}.$

Let's see how with an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4241af18-972e-530c-b06b-388437001b24" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10692 :tutorial/title "Function of a Jordan Decomposition"} :step/id #uuid "82e8fc5c-326f-538e-acdc-fbdce35a6bb4" :step/math-academy-id 231918 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158098}} {:db/id 17592186158098 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157271 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157038 :question/id #uuid "6b751a5e-56c2-5ef0-a640-b77793aa1a72" :question/math-academy-id "e-16517"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "706303c1-0e4c-55f7-8b62-5094938f85bc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048638} {:db/id 17592186049113} {:db/id 17592186049678}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157693} {:db/id 17592186157694} {:db/id 17592186292555} {:db/id 17592186292559} {:db/id 17592186292561} {:db/id 17592186363647} {:db/id 17592186390485} {:db/id 17592186390492} {:db/id 17592186390499} {:db/id 17592186414004}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Decomposition"} :step/id #uuid "62349611-970a-5bd8-b8c7-3d773fb63239" :step/math-academy-id 231919} {:db/id 17592186158424 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158466 :tutorial/content "Consider a Jordan matrix formed by the direct sum of blocks $J_{n_1}(\lambda_1) {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} \cdots {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} J_{n_k}(\lambda_k)$ and a function $f.$ By applying the rule for diagonal matrices to this block diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1})\,⊕\,⋯\,⊕\,{J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k})) & =f(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & {J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k})\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1})) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & f({J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k}))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1}))\,⊕\,⋯\,⊕\,f({J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k})).\end{aligned}
$$

This allows us to compute functions of any matrix in Jordan Normal Form by applying the function to each Jordan block individually.

For example, suppose $J = J_2(2) \oplus J_1(3).$ Then, applying a function $f,$ we have

$$
\begin{bmatrix}f({J}_{2}(2)) & 0 \\ 0 & f({J}_{1}(3))\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e85abcea-5a44-50b9-9104-b71309622287" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14947 :tutorial/title "Function of a Jordan Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "b87874f9-2306-59b4-a907-b5f36d18a293" :step/math-academy-id 610975 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158095}}] :activity/title "Matrix Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157520} {:db/id 17592186158091 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158432 :tutorial/content "We can extend a scalar function $f(x)$ to a square matrix argument $A.$ This function $f(A)$ is called a **matrix function**, and maps a square matrix to another square matrix of the same size.

Given a square matrix $A$ and a scalar function $f$ with Maclaurin series

$$
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k,
$$

we can define $f(A)$ by replacing $x$ with $A,$ with addition and multiplication performed in the matrix sense:

$$
f(A) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k A^k
$$

For example, recall that the Maclaurin series of $f(x) = e^x$ is

$$
e^x = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \dfrac{x^k}{k!}.
$$

Then, for a square matrix $A,$ we define the matrix exponential as

$$

Given a square matrix $A$ and a scalar function $f$ with Maclaurin series

$$
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k,
$$

we can define $f(A)$ by replacing $x$ with $A,$ with addition and multiplication performed in the matrix sense:

$$
f(A) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k A^k
$$

For example, recall that the Maclaurin series of $f(x) = e^x$ is

$$
e^x = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \dfrac{x^k}{k!}.
$$

Then, for a square matrix $A,$ we define the matrix exponential as

$$
e^A = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \dfrac{1}{k!}A^k.
$$

In the next slide, we'll see how to apply matrix functions to square matrices." :tutorial/id #uuid "c3451824-f52b-539c-b16f-3819d3ea37df" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10688 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186158092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158433 :tutorial/content "Suppose $D$ is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}\end{bmatrix}
$$

For a scalar function $f$ with a Maclaurin series expansion, $f(D)$ is the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $f(\lambda_1), \ldots, f(\lambda_n){:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}f({\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & f({\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{bmatrix}
$$

For example, given the matrix
$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
and the function $f(x) = e^x,$ we have

$$
\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & 0 \\ 0 & f(1)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This rule works because raising a diagonal matrix to a power is equivalent to raising each diagonal entry to the same power.

Indeed, if
$\displaystyle
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k$
is the Maclaurin series of $f,$ then, by the definition of $f(D),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(D) & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{D}^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}\end{bmatrix}}^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}^{k}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{n}^{k}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}f({\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & f({\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da162714-f641-5ded-aec8-6f24c0d5cbb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10689 :tutorial/title "Function of a Diagonal Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "c8b4e298-ed67-50ea-bb52-8968e4cd58bf" :step/math-academy-id 231907 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158093}} {:db/id 17592186158433 :tutorial/content "Suppose $D$ is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda  & 1 & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda  & 1 & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & \lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

For a scalar function $f$ analytic at $\lambda$ (i.e., has a Taylor series expansion at $\lambda$), $f(J_n(\lambda))$ is the matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{''}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}
$$

To demonstrate, let's find $f(J_3(2))$ for $f(x) = \ln x.$

Since $J_3(2)$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, we will need the first $3-1=2$ derivatives of $f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}x \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{''}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

![](images/43/439d1a1c3c2c315510fd293e8bb8e1467e149222025359a0e0d899270eb07e12.svg)

Now that we can compute the value of a function of a Jordan block, we can also find the value of a function of a Jordan matrix.

The matrix [math]f(J_n(\lambda))[/math] for [math]n=2,3,[/math] and [math]4[/math] are as follows.

* For [math]2\times 2[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_2(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

* For [math]3\times 3[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_3(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

* For [math]4\times 4[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_4(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) & \dfrac16f'''(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & 0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]" :tutorial/id #uuid "7972371e-9205-5e74-b277-6dfcab332f9b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10691 :tutorial/title "Function of a Jordan Block"} :step/id #uuid "deee50a7-b19c-5fb9-80a5-a024ec3943c0" :step/math-academy-id 231911 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158424}} {:db/id 17592186158434 :tutorial/content "Suppose $J_n(\lambda)$ is an $n\times n$ Jordan block where the main diagonal entries are all $\lambda{:}$

$$

$$

Now that we can compute the value of a function of a Jordan block, we can also find the value of a function of a Jordan matrix.

The matrix [math]f(J_n(\lambda))[/math] for [math]n=2,3,[/math] and [math]4[/math] are as follows.

* For [math]2\times 2[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_2(\lambda)) =

* For [math]4\times 4[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[

\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) & \dfrac16f'''(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & 0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]" :tutorial/id #uuid "7972371e-9205-5e74-b277-6dfcab332f9b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10691 :tutorial/title "Function of a Jordan Block"} {:db/id 17592186158424 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158466 :tutorial/content "Consider a Jordan matrix formed by the direct sum of blocks $J_{n_1}(\lambda_1) {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} \cdots {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} J_{n_k}(\lambda_k)$ and a function $f.$ By applying the rule for diagonal matrices to this block diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1})\,⊕\,⋯\,⊕\,{J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k})) & =f(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & {J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k})\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1})) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & f({J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k}))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\lambda }_{1}))\,⊕\,⋯\,⊕\,f({J}_{{n}_{k}}({\lambda }_{k})).\end{aligned}
$$

For a scalar function $f$ with a Maclaurin series expansion, we have

$$
f(SAS^{-1}) = Sf(A)S^{-1}.
$$

Indeed, given the Maclaurin series $\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_kx^k,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(SA{S}^{-1}) & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}(SA{S}^{-1})^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}S{A}^{k}{S}^{-1} \\  & =S({\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{A}^{k}){S}^{-1} \\  & =Sf(A){S}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So far, we have seen how to evaluate functions for diagonal matrices and Jordan blocks. With the formula above, we will now be able to

- evaluate $f(B)$ for diagonalizable $B$ using a diagonalization $B=PDP^{-1},$ and

- evaluate $f(B)$ for non-diagonalizable $B$ using a Jordan decomposition $B=PJP^{-1}.$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))} & ={e}^{(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}(3) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(0)\end{bmatrix})} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{({J}_{1}(3))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Given that $B=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find ${e}^{B}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and the given matrix $B,$ we have

$$
{e}^{B}={e}^{PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $3$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=\begin{bmatrix}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)={e}^{x}.$ So, we get

$$
{e}^{J}=\begin{bmatrix}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2\cdot 1-3\cdot 1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{B} & =P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & {e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & -2{e}^{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3} & -4{e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & -{e}^{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e83cd1cd-0cd6-5847-8ebe-90dbcdc74de7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414009}} {:db/id 17592186414011 :step/content {:db/id 17592186414004 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "086b5f8c-361e-5e84-ba7f-07908a6ffad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-92 & 62 \\ -186 & 125\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413955} {:answer/id #uuid "5f32c9ba-7882-5683-b822-c627858b4d7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}72 & -52 \\ -166 & 75\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413962} {:answer/id #uuid "6915da6f-7547-5e67-bf4a-3730ded795b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}62 & 92 \\ -125 & 186\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413964} {:answer/id #uuid "774e359d-a732-5eac-9259-4f31c4ad4889" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}32 & 24 \\ -18 & 180\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413970} {:answer/id #uuid "8e0c78fd-212a-50ef-8305-029fa98e0cf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}31 & 46 \\ -67 & 98\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413973}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413955} :answer-field/id #uuid "d52e4f2e-ac8e-5bd0-a3c8-e99ceefdc963" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186413997}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5a76ab5b-a059-5458-b5f4-e674816ed366" :question/math-academy-id "q-253488" :question/problem "Consider the following matrices:

Given that $X=PD{P}^{-1},$ find ${X}^{5}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={x}^{5}$ and the given matrix $X,$ we have

$$
{X}^{5}=(PD{P}^{-1})^{5}=P\cdot ({D}^{5})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
{D}^{5}=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{5} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{5}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 32\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{2}{2\cdot 1-3\cdot 1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$

$$

$$

$$

|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $n=3,$ and $\lambda =2.$

Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first $3-1=2$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(2)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(2) \\ 0 & f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{8} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "67945b3f-2216-5dac-be50-954f07e6800a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414011}} {:db/id 17592186414011 :step/content {:db/id 17592186414004 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "086b5f8c-361e-5e84-ba7f-07908a6ffad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-92 & 62 \\ -186 & 125\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413955} {:answer/id #uuid "5f32c9ba-7882-5683-b822-c627858b4d7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}72 & -52 \\ -166 & 75\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413962} {:answer/id #uuid "6915da6f-7547-5e67-bf4a-3730ded795b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}62 & 92 \\ -125 & 186\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413964} {:answer/id #uuid "774e359d-a732-5eac-9259-4f31c4ad4889" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}32 & 24 \\ -18 & 180\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413970} {:answer/id #uuid "8e0c78fd-212a-50ef-8305-029fa98e0cf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}31 & 46 \\ -67 & 98\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186413973}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413955} :answer-field/id #uuid "d52e4f2e-ac8e-5bd0-a3c8-e99ceefdc963" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186413997}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5a76ab5b-a059-5458-b5f4-e674816ed366" :question/math-academy-id "q-253488" :question/problem "Consider the following matrices:

$$

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(\pi )\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi ))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(\pi ),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\pi )) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\pi )\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\pi )) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6490f6a7-a2fa-5388-aee9-2fd4430c4a1f"} {:db/id 17592186553631 :step/content {:db/id 17592186363647 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5526c323-a2c1-5c5b-97ef-7fe8dc93120e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186363649} {:answer/id #uuid "047b15e1-e229-59bd-ae6f-4c8c03b091db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186363650} {:answer/id #uuid "4de571fa-6b40-524d-9743-5964efb8c012" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186363651} {:answer/id #uuid "cdd35503-f16c-5a9e-8b68-9a58e3b5810d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186363652} {:answer/id #uuid "c854110d-1b0f-5794-affe-f3486969e32d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186363653}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186363649} :answer-field/id #uuid "c4428f89-e5a9-5f0c-ab0a-de1fa79f0c7a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186363648}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "260b8d2c-8f9e-56a2-81b8-5ecd16019589" :question/math-academy-id "q-253493" :question/problem "Consider the following matrices:

$$
E=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,J=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $E=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $E,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $2$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).$ So, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 3-1\cdot 2}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}cos(\pi E) & =P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi J))\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "72a96283-220e-5289-b060-a3483006b0f8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186553625}} {:db/id 17592186553654 :step/content {:db/id 17592186292559 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "137e534f-bd6f-5c02-a6f5-0e5fdadf5e06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}." :db/id 17592186290713} {:answer/id #uuid "462c0bc3-ae5d-5e7d-ba6c-584073583cc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}." :db/id 17592186290921} {:answer/id #uuid "70f6d2e4-7bdd-5df2-a189-1ec0ba9e8bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}." :db/id 17592186291116} {:answer/id #uuid "a0ea62a0-6627-5db1-881f-af6d402bcf16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}." :db/id 17592186291333} {:answer/id #uuid "b6f2e637-dd26-5470-a0dc-0787ea0ddf23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}." :db/id 17592186291424}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186291424} :answer-field/id #uuid "be47bb85-4317-5a50-92bc-2c97250cebc4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186292320}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "dbb79f16-63e6-597b-b683-9d7f2d6be154" :question/math-academy-id "q-253480" :question/problem "Consider the following matrices:

$$

Given that $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡C.$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡C$ and the given matrix $C,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡C=\operatorname{cos}⁡(PD{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡D=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-2\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡C & =P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

"Consider the following matrices:

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}\pi  & 2\pi  \\ 0 & 2\pi \end{bmatrix},\,D=\begin{bmatrix}\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & 2\pi \end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡C.$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡C$ and the given matrix $C,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡C=\operatorname{cos}⁡(PD{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡D=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-2\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡C & =P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "98382843-44b7-53a8-b1a3-61c2c6739e6c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186553631}} {:db/id 17592186553625 :step/content {:db/id 17592186377013 :question/answer-fields $$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
E=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,J=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $E=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $E,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $2$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).$ So, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 3-1\cdot 2}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then what is $x_1+x_2?$" :question/worked-solution "If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=5 \\ -{x}_{1} &=-5 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we obtain $x_1=5,$ which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ 4(5)+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ {x}_{2} & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15$ into the third equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 3(5)+(-15) & =0 \\ 0 & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15,$ which means

$$
5 \mathbf{c_1}-15 \mathbf{c_2} = \mathbf{d}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2=5-15=-10.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186535346} {:db/id 17592186120293 :question/id #uuid "b9323edd-e697-569c-8dd2-3fe5f9eed059" :question/math-academy-id "q-34054"} {:db/id 17592186120350 :question/id #uuid "14248ec5-b54c-565b-8b43-275a9e097f62" :question/math-academy-id "q-34568"} {:db/id 17592186240990 :question/id #uuid "a4963b43-3177-544a-ab68-1ea699a13395" :question/math-academy-id "q-105166" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "222862ae-7c2b-5d66-9d9a-f59640c9801e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186238354} {:answer/id #uuid "346bdb71-8966-5ed4-ab2e-83d1ea69e239" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186238507} {:answer/id #uuid "4072326e-9528-5390-aaaa-546988c57563" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186238613} {:answer/id #uuid "4f101a20-f607-5e7e-b164-71aebdad2935" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186238733} {:answer/id #uuid "61153d6d-bad7-5e46-a284-cae191fc9a25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186238908}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238507} :answer-field/id #uuid "47a0ee5a-75fc-5e2b-8002-cf62c42bfe1d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240456}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{2} \\ 5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the resulting equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3(-5) & =1 \\ -2{x}_{1} & =-14 \\ {x}_{1} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 3(7)+5(-5) & =-4 \\ -4 & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5,$ which means

$$
7{a}_{1}-5{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ -1 \\ -18\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}5{x}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ -1 \\ -18\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ -1 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=16 \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} &=-1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=-18\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $3$, the second equation by $2$, and adding the resulting equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}15{x}_{2}+8{x}_{2} & =48-2 \\ 23{x}_{2} & =46 \\ {x}_{2} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{2}=2$  into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} & =-1\text{ } \\ 3{x}_{1}+4(2) & =-1 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =-9 \\ {x}_{1} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=-3$ and ${x}_{2}=2$ into our third equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} & =-18 \\ 4(-3)-3(2) & =-18 \\ -18 & =-18,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement.

$$

$$

If $x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 + x_3\mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf b,$ then what is $x_1+x_2+x_3?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $\mathbf{b}$ is a linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{a_1}, \,\mathbf{a_2}$ and $\mathbf{a_3}$ with coefficients $x_1,\, x_2$ and $x_3,$ respectively, we have

\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

![](images/9b/9bf913744317fab321cf9f2e01da732853a52a4fd7948c65da596ae4706f6dce.svg)

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $x_3 = 2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_2 = -1,
$$

and substituting $x_3=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1+2(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_1 = -3.
$$

So the solution of the system is $x_1=-3, x_2=-1, x_3=2,$ which means

$$
-3 \mathbf{a_1}- \mathbf{a_2} +2 \mathbf{a_3}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2+x_3=-3-1+2=-2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186538215} {:db/id 17592186120309 :question/id #uuid "6f395246-75c5-52ab-b275-6f768034cd27" :question/math-academy-id "q-34243" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119854 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "13a44dc8-4699-519f-8cb1-87ad77471ebe" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for Three Coefficients in a Linear Combination"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8747e1ec-5bdc-5604-985b-58468728da61" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-11" :db/id 17592186117994} {:answer/id #uuid "bf310542-d18d-58a7-8e58-a22420156a7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186117995} {:answer/id #uuid "cc90ae26-d46f-5f50-bd00-0e92bd416881" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "17" :db/id 17592186117996} {:answer/id #uuid "5599f481-dd85-552e-af10-eea6867254c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186117997} {:answer/id #uuid "71e2eba5-06c7-50b6-88b0-7ea8c256dfb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186117998}] :answer-field/id #uuid "c343bbfd-7cc0-5884-946e-aa6090814a96" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186117993}] :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

"Consider the vectors

$$

$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{2} \\ 5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the resulting equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3(-5) & =1 \\ -2{x}_{1} & =-14 \\ {x}_{1} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 3(7)+5(-5) & =-4 \\ -4 & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5,$ which means

$$
7{a}_{1}-5{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=7+(-5)=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "130d098a-c26b-57ed-9a17-40b7cc7b707e"} {:db/id 17592186435827 :step/content {:db/id 17592186435824 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b3b3e4e-ca03-5bf0-b918-e879378cf4f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186435813} {:answer/id #uuid "3e56b548-f823-5efc-89ba-5bfa7fe486df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186435814} {:answer/id #uuid "62cff3cd-01fc-5c8d-bb73-00c6490598f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-11" :db/id 17592186435815} {:answer/id #uuid "7f4f8e1e-a357-552c-aea0-48de6f4f316a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" :db/id 17592186435817} {:answer/id #uuid "a0c118c7-81b9-5bfc-90ce-dd9634f5f92e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186435820}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435814} :answer-field/id #uuid "a66e7a5d-9617-5080-a5e0-b50e86007465" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435823}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e8bdc664-5423-57fc-a753-871b318d24e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-34598" :question/problem "Find the value of ${x}_{1}-{x}_{2}$ given that  $4a+3x=b$ and

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ -2{x}_{2}-11{x}_{3} &=-18 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -15 & -30\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{15}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ {x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=-6 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this value into  the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}-2(2)=-6\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-2.
$$

 

Finally, by substituting ${x}_{2}=-2$ and ${x}_{3}=2$ into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} & =5 \\ {x}_{1}+(-2)+3(2) & =5 \\ {x}_{1}+4 & =5 \\ {x}_{1} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=1$, ${x}_{2}=-2$, and ${x}_{3}=2,$ which means 

$$
{a}_{1}-2{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1+(-2)+2=1.

Here, we know that the hypotenuse has length $2.$ So, if the length of a leg is $a,$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a \\ a & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the square root from the denominator, we can multiply both the numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{2\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
AB=BC=a.
$$

$$
AC=AB\cdot \sqrt{2}=a\sqrt{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 10+5\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 5(2+\sqrt{2}) & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 5(2+\sqrt{2}) & =(2+\sqrt{2})a \\ 5\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})}a \\ 5 & =a.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p=15 \\ p+2q=9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

$$
\begin{aligned}5b+25 & =0 \\ 5b & =-25 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-5) & =6a+14 \\ -10 & =6a+14 \\ -10-14 & =6a \\ 6a & =-24 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
a+b=-4+(-5)=-4-5=-9.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048646} {:db/id 17592186048873} {:db/id 17592186048975} {:db/id 17592186048991} {:db/id 17592186049144} {:db/id 17592186049198} {:db/id 17592186049869} {:db/id 17592186050326} The number of subscribers increased by $35%$ per year until $2005.$ How many cell-phone subscribers were there in $2005?$" :question/worked-solution "The number of subscribers $y(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $35%.$

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
y=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

We have:

- $a=5\,000$ is the initial number of subscribers.

- $r=0.35$ is the growth rate ($35%$ expressed as a decimal).

- $t=$ the time, in years.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5\,000\cdot (1+0.35)^{t} \\  & =5\,000\cdot (1.35)^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the expression for the number of subscribers after $15$ years, we get

$$
y(15)=5,000\cdot (1.35)^{15}≈450\,792.
$$

$$

$$

According to this model, how many views are there estimated to be after $3$ hours?" :question/worked-solution "The number of views $V(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $120%.$

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=50$ is the total number of views initially

- $r=1.2$ is the growth rate ($120%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t=$ the time (in hours) after the video was posted

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
V=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

Therefore, the correct expression for $V(t)$ is

$$
V=50\cdot (1+1.2)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
V(t)=50\cdot (2.2)^{t}.
$$

To find the total number of views after $3$ hours, we evaluate the above for $t=3:$

$$
V(3)=50\cdot (2.2)^{3}≈532
$$

Therefore, the estimated number of views after $3$ hours is $532.$"} {:db/id 17592186500323 :question/id #uuid "7b3a2ac3-80ac-548f-ab31-d1de79eaa643" :question/math-academy-id "q-318202" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "421513ab-7ba9-53ad-8cc4-202843fff382" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499779} {:answer/id #uuid "49751aae-f779-5ca6-9b9e-7a8ffe15ccc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (2.9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499793} {:answer/id #uuid "77ce4af4-fcc6-55af-ac0a-de8056e6b319" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (3.9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499875} {:answer/id #uuid "961d3d8b-abcf-51c0-a2d4-4c9ea00eafc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (0.9)^{t}" :db/id 17592186499947} {:answer/id #uuid "fffde48d-2021-53c1-b6ab-24b4f090abde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "V(t)=40\cdot (19)^{t}" :db/id 17592186500177}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499793} :answer-field/id #uuid "8f647258-0007-5333-ac78-26a8426f4858" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186500237}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "When a new article was first published on a news website, it had $40$ views. Let's write down what we know:

- $a=40$ is the total number of views initially

- $r=1.9$ is the growth rate ($190%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t=$ the time (in hours) after publication

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
V=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

Therefore, the correct expression for $V(t)$ is

$$
V=40\cdot (1+1.9)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
V(t)=40\cdot (2.9)^{t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186551241 :question/id #uuid "1818fb31-e6dd-51ed-98a5-48141bc40666" :question/math-academy-id "q-318203"} {:db/id 17592186048650} {:db/id 17592186049090} {:db/id 17592186050772} "There is a proportional relationship between a distance in miles $(m)$ and the same distance in yards $(y)$:

| Miles ($m$) | Yards ($y$) |
| --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1\,760$ |
| $2$ | $3\,520$ |
| $3$ | $5\,280$ |

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The unit rate is $1\,760$ yards per mile.

II. There are $3\,760$ yards in $2$ miles.

III. There are $480$ yards in a quarter of a mile." :question/worked-solution "We're told that $m$ and $y$ have a proportional relationship.

To find the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(m,y)$ from the table. Let's choose the point $(1,1\,760),$  which corresponds to the first row of the table. 

We can find the constant of proportionality as follows:

$$
k=\frac{y}{m}=\frac{1\,760}{1}=1\,760
$$

The units of $k$ are "yards per mile" since we divided the distance in yard $y$  by the distance in miles $m.$ 

Therefore, the relationship between $y$ and $m$ is 

$$
y=1\,760m.
$$

  

Now, with that in mind, let's look at each statement.

- Statement I is true. We found above that $k=1\,760.$

- Statement II is false. The second row of the table corresponds to the point $(2,3\,520)$ which means that there are $3\,520$ yards in $2$ miles, not $3\,760.$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $m=\frac{1}{4}$ into the relationship $y=1\,760m,$ we get 

$$
y=1\,760\cdot \frac{1}{4}=1\,760÷4=440
$$

which means that there are $440$ yards in a quarter of a mile, not $480.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186048993} {:db/id 17592186049141} {:db/id 17592186050890 :topic/id #uuid "6eaa79dd-c90f-5e62-94cb-871b5a23b05e" :topic/knowledge-points Consequently, isosceles right triangles are often called **$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{90^\circ}$ triangles**.

![](images/d3/d32159528abc75f3ed8bcccaedb2765b676fd6cc64164e2f8c81f98eb37f6db4.png)

All $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles share a special property:

*In any ${45^\circ}$-${45^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the length of the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.*

To see why this is, remember that

- in an isosceles triangle, the two legs must have the same length, and

- in a right triangle, the square of the longest side must equal the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides.

So, if an isosceles right triangle has legs of length $a$ and the hypotenuse has length $h,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{a}^{2} \\ {h}^{2} & =2{a}^{2} \\ h & =\sqrt{2{a}^{2}} \\ h & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7e5fefd4-4ac4-5999-8c6d-0ad927da9ca6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2381 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8b5ee65a-7747-5a0e-9d06-721118b74e10" :step/math-academy-id 10416 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060461}} {:db/id 17592186060461 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059630 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059462 :question/id #uuid "d1277863-7d33-566d-91b9-7a78458dca8e" :question/math-academy-id "e-3077"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "73ad4cd2-e7f0-5b7d-82fc-1a8e4b0597d8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060289} {:db/id 17592186060290} {:db/id 17592186497361} {:db/id 17592186497375}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of the Hypotenuse of a 45-45-90 Triangle Given the Legs"} :step/id #uuid "0b3e5ddd-300e-5258-b19c-3499c565bdad" :step/math-academy-id 10419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060462}} {:db/id 17592186060462 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059631 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059463 :question/id #uuid "ce112319-10a9-5483-82c3-566c0630b23a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3080"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5faa905-dcfc-5eed-b4ed-5818ca6ef342" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048702}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060096} {:db/id 17592186060282} {:db/id 17592186497351} {:db/id 17592186497385} {:db/id 17592186508040}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of the Legs of a 45-45-90 Triangle Given the Hypotenuse"} :step/id #uuid "7049be2a-b0af-5170-a1cb-c440a35c6663" :step/math-academy-id 10420 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060473}} {:db/id 17592186060468 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060873 :tutorial/content "Now that we know about $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles, it's straightforward to see that the diagonal of any square is $\sqrt{2}$ times the side length of the square.

$$

Here, we know that the hypotenuse has length $2.$ So, if the length of a leg is $a,$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a \\ a & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the square root from the denominator, we can multiply both the numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{2\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}

a wildlife reserve. If the deer population doubles every year, can we find a function that gives the number of deer after $t$ years? 

First, let's write down what we know:

- $a = 120$ is the **initial number** of deer

- $b =2$ is the **growth factor** (equal to $2$ because the number of deer doubles every year)

- $t=$ the time (in years)

We let $y(t)$ be the number of deer in the reserve after $t$ years.  The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = ab^t.
$$

Substituting our values for $a$ and $b,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 120\cdot 2^t.
$$

We can use this formula to find the number of deer in the reserve for any value of $t \geq 0.$ For example, to find the number of deer after $3$ years, we substitute $t=3$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =120\cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =120\cdot 8 \\  & =960\end{aligned}
$$

So there will be $960$ deer after $3$ years.

Finally, notice that substituting $t=0$ into the formula gives the initial number of deer:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =120\cdot {2}^{0} \\  & =120\cdot 1 \\  & =120\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ed1b9eba-931a-5908-99c6-58b738afef7d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1937 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "642a7826-566a-5e56-b810-cb6fb7d5fa0c" :step/math-academy-id 531824 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148357}} {:db/id 17592186148357 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147473 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147198 :question/id #uuid "7e261e75-a3ec-59cf-a7b7-ad935cb4e55d" :question/math-academy-id "e-1987"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "80c3fbf3-5165-510f-b130-d216d5c8aa19" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049619} {:db/id 17592186050886}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147898} {:db/id 17592186147910} {:db/id 17592186489214} {:db/id 17592186489253}] :knowledge-point/title "Modeling Exponential Growth Using a Growth Factor"} :step/id #uuid "c0ba8192-ba62-514c-b119-d4b80274d19c" :step/math-academy-id 531825 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148358}} {:db/id 17592186148358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148683 :tutorial/content "When dealing with exponential growth, it's more common to be given a **growth rate** instead of a growth factor. A growth rate is usually expressed as a percent.

For example, suppose that an investor invests $\[math]500$ dollars in the shares of some high-growth companies. It's expected that the investment will grow by $35\%$ each year. Can we write a function that describes the value of the investment after $t$ years? 

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=\[/math]500$ is the **initial value** of the investment

- $r = 0.35$ is the **growth rate** (this is simply $35\%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t$ is the time (in years)

Let $y(t)$ be the value of the investment after $t$ years. The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y = a(1+r)^t.
$$

Substituting in our values for $a$ and $r,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 500(1+0.35)^t.
$$

Simplifying the above, we arrive at

$$
y(t) = 500(1.35)^t.
$$

When creating exponential growth functions, the key takeaway is this:

- If you're given a **growth rate** $r$ (usually expressed as a percent), then use the formula $y = a(1+r)^t.$

- If you're given a **growth factor** $b,$ then use the formula $y = ab^t.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65e48fd4-d6c3-5e02-aad1-9a8dae46b0bf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1936 :tutorial/title "Modeling A growth rate is usually expressed as a percent.

For example, suppose that an investor invests $\[math]500$ dollars in the shares of some high-growth companies. It's expected that the investment will grow by $35\%$ each year. Can we write a function that describes the value of the investment after $t$ years? 

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=\[/math]500$ is the **initial value** of the investment

- $r = 0.35$ is the **growth rate** (this is simply $35\%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t$ is the time (in years)

Let $y(t)$ be the value of the investment after $t$ years. The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y = a(1+r)^t.
$$

Substituting in our values for $a$ and $r,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 500(1+0.35)^t.
$$

Simplifying the above, we arrive at

$$
y(t) = 500(1.35)^t.
$$

When creating exponential growth functions, the key takeaway is this:

- If you're given a **growth rate** $r$ (usually expressed as a percent), then use the formula $y = a(1+r)^t.$

- If you're given a **growth factor** $b,$ then use the formula $y = ab^t.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65e48fd4-d6c3-5e02-aad1-9a8dae46b0bf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1936 :tutorial/title "Modeling Exponential Growth Using a Growth Rate"} :step/id #uuid "4ad684e1-3cee-5aab-8d3d-e3b084e25e37" :step/math-academy-id 531828 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148359}} {:db/id 17592186148683 :tutorial/content "When dealing with exponential growth, it's more common to be given a **growth rate** instead of a growth factor. According to this estimate, what will be the price of the watch after $3$ decades? Round your answer to the nearest dollar." :question/worked-solution "The price of the watch $y(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $8%.$

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
y=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

We have:

- $a=50$ dollars is the original price of the watch.

- $r=0.08$ is the growth rate ($8%$ expressed as a decimal).

- $t=$ the time, in decades.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =50\cdot (1+0.08)^{t} \\  & =50\cdot (1.08)^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the function at $t=3$ gives the value of the watch after $3$ decades.

$$
y(3)=50\cdot (1.08)^{3}≈63
$$

Therefore, the value of the watch after $3$ decades will be approximately $$63.$"} :step/id #uuid "d0fc5aff-4ed7-58b6-9140-1572b6374187" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500427}} {:db/id 17592186500427 :step/content {:db/id 17592186500311 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6885483a-aa71-5fea-be44-2ce9914f562d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "86" :db/id 17592186499854} {:answer/id #uuid "99d3b702-8f26-5fec-864d-fc1d46d65b97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "700" :db/id 17592186499952} {:answer/id #uuid "a54c4dd1-562b-5848-ac11-19e631519c9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "532" :db/id 17592186499977} {:answer/id #uuid "ab6b2e34-5b0d-511b-9c71-0da9a7de6e76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "246" :db/id 17592186499993} {:answer/id #uuid "be53aed4-2603-538a-bb13-6ffecb59a0fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "198" :db/id 17592186500043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499977} :answer-field/id #uuid "1232ee90-f900-5499-a331-ceb50d527115" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186500188}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "50e1b98c-c8a1-53cf-8367-e3764f5a2f08" :question/math-academy-id "q-317613" :question/problem "A video was posted on a streaming platform with $50$ initial views. According to this model, how many views are there estimated to be after $3$ hours?" :question/worked-solution "The number of views $V(t)$ grows exponentially with a growth rate of $120%.$

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=50$ is the total number of views initially

- $r=1.2$ is the growth rate ($120%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t=$ the time (in hours) after the video was posted

The formula for exponential growth (in terms of a growth rate $r$) is

$$
V=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

Therefore, the correct expression for $V(t)$ is

$$
V=50\cdot (1+1.2)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
V(t)=50\cdot (2.2)^{t}.
$$

To find the total number of views after $3$ hours, we evaluate the above for $t=3:$

$$
V(3)=50\cdot (2.2)^{3}≈532
$$

Therefore, the estimated number of views after $3$ hours is $532.$"} :step/id #uuid "99c28962-0c9b-59a2-8213-fe4b9b34df2d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500399}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=4 \\ x-2 &=y\,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable." :tutorial/id #uuid "e1e8cb2d-3d4e-5cb9-8947-2bd9deb11b89" "5c71bd6b-b9a3-5587-89f4-a14a2c760bc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-5179" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $p-q?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p=15 \\ p+2q=9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $p$ by dividing both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p & =15 \\ p & =5\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $p=5$ into $p+2q=9,$ then we can find the value of $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p+2q & =9 \\ (5)+2q & =9 \\ 2q & =4 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=5,\,q=2.$ So,

$$
p-q=5-2=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0a9225c0-5f39-5569-928a-3834451e9d52" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547152}} {:db/id 17592186547152 :step/content {:db/id 17592186546991 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b85cb2c-460d-5f91-86c0-674d13fae83e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186546309} {:answer/id #uuid "242eed59-c937-5dab-b478-b3a1accb9d4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186546329} {:answer/id #uuid "463e0a8b-5e11-54a2-8cdd-72b176626176" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186546407} {:answer/id #uuid "6a785a85-c477-5db9-a10d-570f963f9181" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186546485} {:answer/id #uuid "f5ff80ce-ffb0-542a-ba50-ce8557612884" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186546805}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186546309} :answer-field/id #uuid "e282d81b-1bfe-5c5b-abe6-d91779057814" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186546940}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3b789afd-79c7-56fc-b94a-f894f177dfe2" :question/math-academy-id "q-18555" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a+b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 \\ 5b+25=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 & \,\,(1) \\ 5b+25=0. & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can solve for $b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b+25 & =0 \\ 5b & =-25 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $b=-5$ into equation $(1)$ and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-5) & =6a+14 \\ -10 & =6a+14 \\ -10-14 & =6a \\ 6a & =-24 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=-5.$ So,

$$
a+b=-4+(-5)=-4-5=-9.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ca7de6ad-e459-52ba-851d-06dd86cc6059" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547164}} {:db/id 17592186547164 :step/content {:db/id 17592186546971 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25d7a53c-5916-5db7-992b-ff7a626a51c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186546336} {:answer/id #uuid "51399b6f-2763-5014-9b02-635633f0dada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186546427} {:answer/id #uuid "9e23c320-e17b-534f-8a91-354568ebc163" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186546603} {:answer/id #uuid "a3f272eb-ffc1-5fb6-b622-055a0def12d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186546617} {:answer/id #uuid "d9f37f2b-79d8-5ebd-8615-8e1bcfb28380" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186546732}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186546732} :answer-field/id #uuid "78ca5c4c-b502-5598-a6f0-d81d606b319e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186546881}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1ad70587-af92-55e0-95cf-31aa82c10e13" :question/math-academy-id "q-52115" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a-b?$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186153033 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153438 :tutorial/content "Two variables, $x$ and $y,$ are said to have a **proportional relationship** if their ratio is constant. That is, for any $(x,y)$ pair, we have

$$
k = \dfrac{y}{x}
$$

where $k$ is a fixed number called the **constant of proportionality** or **constant of variation.**

As a concrete example, let's consider the table below. 

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ |
| $2$ | $4$ |
| $4$ | $8$ |

Do $x$ and $y$ have a proportional relationship?

 What is the value of $x?$

First, note that $\angle DIF$ and $\angle BJI$ are corresponding angles. Therefore, they are congruent and thus have the same measure. This means we can write down the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠DIF & =m∠BJI \\ 3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this equation, we first subtract $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘} \\ 3x-{20}^{∘}-x & =x+{10}^{∘}-x \\ 2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $20^\circ$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘} \\ 2x-{20}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={30}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={30}^{∘} \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{{30}^{∘}}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & ={15}^{∘} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $r$, $s$ and $t$ in the above diagram are parallel, find $m∠v.$" :question/worked-solution "Consider $∠2$ and $∠3$ in the diagram below.

![](images/50/50d1e010a8279bf8f59a5e57b4ee4d4b744af7e431351bb17397e123aa79c59a.png)

Note that $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is ${100}^{∘}$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠2={100}^{∘}.
$$

Similarly, note that $∠3$ and the angle whose measure is ${36}^{∘}$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠3={36}^{∘}.
$$

Let's add these measures to our diagram:

![](images/ce/ce9944a3fa28177bd0882fccd53d544159b6f041c570e7037cac7db31103130e.png)

The angles $∠v$, $∠2,$ and $∠3$ combined give a straight angle. So, we get:

:step/content {:db/id 17592186069956 :tutorial/content "The **circumference** of a circle is the length of the path that goes around the circle.

![](images/ac/ac8f31a99961c51cb53695d9daab017126d1316b720e6383b876824d7c7947bd.png)

The circumference is usually denoted by the letter $C.$

One important fact about the circumference is that, for *any* circle, no matter how small or large it is, the ratio of circumference $C$ to diameter $d$ is a fixed number! Specifically,

$$
\dfrac{C}{d} = {\color{blue}\boldsymbol{\pi}} \approx 3.141\,592\,654...
$$

 

This important irrational number is called **pi** (pronounced "pie") and we use the Greek letter $\pi$ to express it. So, we can calculate the circumference by using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}C=\pi d.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, our circle has diameter $4\,\textrm{cm},$ so its circumference is

$$
C = \pi \cdot 4 = 4\pi \approx 12.566\,\mathrm{cm},
$$

rounded to three decimal digits.

Since the diameter is twice as long as the radius ($d=2r$), we can also write the formula for the circumference as

$$
C = \pi d = 2\pi r.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e75a0c81-7a99-51d8-85ff-de6951125d7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2423 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3437ac3b-f6ef-5e78-8b46-bca7d485abd4" :step/math-academy-id
